Why does your child sleep with an open mouth?

• Broken sleep, snoring, night sweats: A child who breathes through the mouth often sleeps restlessly, snores and sweats at night.
• Tired and distracted at school: Poor sleep is linked with daytime tiredness and trouble concentrating.
• Dry mouth, bad breath, cavities: Breathing through the mouth dries it out, which can mean bad breath and more cavities.
• Repeated tonsil and nose infections: Blocked noses and enlarged tonsils often go together with mouth breathing.
• Mood and behaviour: Irritability and restlessness are linked with poor sleep. Linked does not mean proven cause.

Mouth breathing in a child: what happens years later?

• A low tongue and a narrow palate: When the tongue does not rest on the palate, the upper jaw may not widen as it should.
• A long face and a set-back lower jaw: Long-term mouth breathing is associated with a longer face and a lower jaw that sits back.
• Crowded teeth, longer orthodontics: A narrow jaw leaves less room, so teeth crowd and braces may take longer.
• A narrow airway that grows with them: A narrow airway in childhood can stay narrow in adulthood and affect sleep.
• Why early assessment matters: A growing child responds best to early guidance. Waiting leaves fewer options, and it can affect the child's health and healthy growth.

Is your child a mouth breather? A quick checklist

• Mouth open at rest: Watch your child while watching TV or sleeping. Is the mouth open most of the time?
• Snoring and morning tiredness: Loud snoring, restless sleep and a hard time waking up are worth noting.
• Is it only a look?: Dark circles and a long, narrow face are not only about appearance. They can point to disturbed growth and a problem in general health.
• Spaced or crowded teeth: Teeth that are crowded or spaced out may point to how the jaw and tongue are working.
• A blocked nose all the time: A nose that is always blocked pushes a child to breathe through the mouth.

Two or more signs? See your doctor for an assessment.

No sleep apnea, but your brain keeps waking up

• What it is: UARS: the airway is narrow but does not fully close, so the brain wakes up to keep breathing.
• 10 or more arousals an hour: In published criteria, 10 or more breathing-related arousals per hour point to UARS.
• Who it affects: It is often described in young, slim adults and in women, who rarely look like the typical apnea patient.
• Symptoms: Tiredness, headaches and trouble sleeping are common.
• Why it goes unnoticed for years: A normal apnea index can hide it, so it needs a study that measures breathing effort.

Reference: Guilleminault; Stoohs 2007. A diagnosis needs a lab study.

Reading an 8-hour sleep study

• Breathing index: 1.6: An AHI of 1.6 is normal. On breathing pauses alone, this night looks fine.
• But the sleep itself is not normal: Only light sleep stages. No real deep sleep at all. The body was in bed for 8 hours, but it is as if it never slept.
• Zero minutes of deep sleep: From this study. Typical adults spend only a small share of the night in stage 1 and a much larger share in deep sleep.
• What deep sleep does: Deep sleep helps the brain store memories and clear waste, and helps the body repair itself and regulate hormones and blood sugar.
• When deep sleep stays missing: Studies link long-term loss of deep sleep with memory problems, higher blood pressure, blood sugar changes and a higher dementia risk. The longer it lasts, the more it matters.

Blood pressure peaks during sleep

• Peak: 258/146 mmHg: 258 is the highest systolic pressure recorded during the night: the pressure when the heart pushes blood out.
• What sleep should look like: Asleep, blood pressure usually falls and stays below about 120/80, and the heart rate often settles around 50 to 60 beats per minute.
• Heart rate: up to 140: While asleep, the pulse reached 140 beats per minute. That is the rate of someone exercising, not resting.
• Values like these are dangerous: Readings in this range can threaten life and raise the risk of a sudden cardiac or brain event. They are not numbers to wait on.
• The cause in this case: the jaw: In this case, the assessment points to the jaw and airway structure as what disturbs breathing, and so the pressure and pulse, all night.

Why pressure surges when breathing struggles

• A closing airway: When the airway narrows during sleep, the body struggles to get air in.
• The alarm response: The brain fires alarms and the body responds: the heart speeds up abnormally and the blood vessels constrict abnormally, to make up for the lack of oxygen across the whole body.
• Pressure jumps: Blood pressure reaches abnormal levels. Time after time, a chronic condition can develop: arterial hypertension, heart failure, or other vascular and blood diseases.
• A link, not a guarantee: Not everyone with a narrow airway reaches extreme values. Each case needs its own measurements.
• Why we measure: A sleep study shows what actually happens at night, not only what we expect.

A heart at 140 beats while you sleep

• Resting versus working: A sleeping heart usually slows down. At 140 beats per minute, you are lying down but doing hard exercise.

• A load on the heart: A peak pressure of 258 means a heavy load on the heart in a single night. Now imagine it repeating every single day.
• Do not ignore it: Unexplained fast pulse or high pressure at night deserves a proper evaluation.
• Look for the cause: Look for the cause instead of taking medication for life. If the cause is structural, there may be a chance to treat the chronic condition at its root, and for good.

Normal at the clinic, abnormal at night

• A daytime reading can mislead: Blood pressure measured while awake can look acceptable even when nights are not.
• Sleep should lower pressure: In healthy sleep, pressure usually dips below the daytime level.
• When it does not dip: If the pressure stays high or surges at night, the heart and vessels get no break.
• Why it matters: Night-time pressure is linked with cardiovascular risk, sometimes more than daytime readings.
• What to do: If you have poor sleep and high pressure, ask for a night-time assessment.
